conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that regular low-dose CT screening in heavy current and former smokers is supported by strong randomized trial evidence and reduces lung cancer-specific mortality by approximately 20%.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
Yes — the evidence from multiple large randomized controlled trials supports this conclusion.

**Key evidence:**

The **National Lung Screening Trial (NLST)**, a large U.S. RCT of heavy current/former smokers, found that annual low-dose CT (LDCT) screening reduced lung cancer mortality by **20.3%** compared to chest X-ray screening ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873); [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/bulletin/2011/ct-scan.html)).

The **NELSON trial**, a European RCT using volume-based CT screening in high-risk former/current smokers, confirmed and extended these findings, showing a "substantially lower lung-cancer mortality than no screening among high-risk persons," with benefits seen in both men and women ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1911793?sort=newest&page=0)).

Based on this trial evidence, the **U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)** concludes "with moderate certainty that annual screening for lung cancer with low-dose computed tomography has a moderate benefit in persons at high risk of lung cancer" based on age and smoking history/exposure, and issued a formal screening recommendation ([USPSTF](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening)).

A pooled meta-analysis of randomized LDCT screening trials (including UKLS, NELSON, and others) further supports a consistent mortality-reduction signal across studies ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8589726/)).

**Caveats:** Benefits are specific to high-risk populations (heavy smoking history, appropriate age range) — screening low-risk individuals is not recommended. Screening also carries harms, including false positives, overdiagnosis, and radiation exposure, which must be weighed against benefits ([lung.org](https://www.lung.org/blog/why-lung-cancer-screening)). Effects on all-cause mortality (versus lung-cancer-specific mortality) remain more debated.

**Conclusion:** Yes — for heavy (ex-)smokers meeting risk criteria, regular LDCT screening is supported by strong randomized trial evidence to reduce lung cancer-specific mortality by roughly 20%.
